title: Genetic control of translational elongation decouples transcriptome and translatome in maize
content:
Abstract
Gene expression is a complex biological process that converts genetic information from DNA into proteins. It is important to emphasize that the extensively utilized transcriptome does not fully capture post-transcriptional regulation, and the translatome can provide additional information about gene expression. In this study, we simultaneously acquired transcriptome and translatome data from a diverse natural maize population, profiling the transcription levels of 28,571 genes across 200 inbred lines and the translation levels of 18,446 genes across 185 inbred lines. Our findings reveal that (i) transcription and translation levels exhibit moderate correlation (median r = 0.44, range −0.47 to 0.95), highlighting the regulatory divergence between these layers; (ii) genetic effects are buffered along the direction of gene expression, from 78.49% at the transcription level to 52.86% at the translation level, while stronger regulatory effects driven by structural variations are more stable across both layers; (iii) coding region mutations specifically modulate translation dynamics by affecting ribosome movement, as reflected in population-wide ribosome pausing variations; and (iv) transcriptional and translational variations can independently explain phenotypic variance. Altogether, this study highlights how genetic mutations shape concordant and discordant expression patterns between the transcriptome and translatome, providing new insights into their regulatory mechanisms and impacts on phenotypic variations.
